cards.text: Brand new book, baker: Proverbs! It opens like the label on a cookie box, telling us whose sayings these are, and he's a king of Israel. Then, before one single proverb, it tells us what the whole book is FOR.

cards.question: These are the proverbs of King ___, son of ___.

cards.text: This book is for gaining wisdom and discipline, for understanding words of insight, and for learning wise living, righteousness, justice and equity. It's the instructions on the box, friend, and unlike me with a brand new oven, you're actually going to READ them.

cards.question: Proverbs says it gives prudence to one group, and knowledge and discretion to another. Who are those two groups?
Proverbs says people who are already wise can skip this book.

cards.text: Even the wise keep growing by understanding proverbs, parables, sayings and the riddles of the wise. RIDDLES, friend, and the mystery key from my old junk drawer, the one that spent YEARS guessing which door it opened, would have LOVED this book.

cards.question: Before a single proverb starts, the book names where knowledge begins. Where?
The flip side of that same line: fools love wisdom and discipline.

cards.text: Then the voice turns personal, telling the son to listen to his father's instruction. Friend, I gave that speech for YEARS, usually to a little cookie cutter wobbling at the edge of the counter.

cards.question: The son is told to listen to his father's instruction. Whose teaching is he told not to forsake?
The son is told to hold on to what his father and mother teach him. What picture does the voice use for that teaching?

cards.text: Now the voice gets serious with the son: sinners might try to entice him. And friend, they are NOT going to show up wearing name tags that say SINNER.

cards.question: If sinners try to entice the son, he's told to hear them out first before he decides.

cards.text: The voice even plays out their pitch. It starts, "Come along, let us lie in wait for blood," and friend, that is NOT an invite you RSVP yes to.

cards.question: In their pitch, the sinners plan to ambush people who are ___, and for no reason at all.

cards.text: They brag they'll swallow their victims alive like Sheol, whole like those going down into the Pit. These guys are not subtle, friend.

cards.question: The sinners are selling this plan hard. They promise they'll fill their ___ with plunder.

cards.text: Then the closer: "Throw in your lot with us; let us all share one purse". Friend, when a crew like THIS says we'll all share one purse, keep one hand on your apron pocket.

cards.question: The son is told it's fine to walk along with these sinners, as long as he skips the ambush.
Why should the son stay off the sinners' path?

cards.text: Then comes a picture from catching birds: "How futile it is to spread the net where any bird can see it!" Hold that picture, friend, because here comes the twist.

cards.question: The sinners talked about lying in wait for blood. Whose blood does the voice say they're lying in wait for?
Ambushing their own lives turns out to be the fate of a certain kind of person. Who?
Unjust gain takes the ___ of the ones who hold it.

findings.problem: The right answer "The fear of the LORD" stands out because it is the only one that sounds like Scripture, with LORD in capitals. "A good teacher" and "A long life" sound like everyday phrases. The baker can pick the Bible-sounding answer without reasoning.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: The question starts "The flip side of that same line," which points back to the line from card 7. That card is no longer on screen, so the baker doesn't know which line it means. The question should name the line itself (the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge).

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: The blank in "fill their ___ with plunder" (houses, tents or wagons) asks the baker to guess the wording of the line. Nothing told so far lets the baker reason out houses over tents or wagons, and the choice doesn't change the meaning.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.
